After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. item.title: Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
item.description:

Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
November 5, 202611:15 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
Comedian and actor Russell Brand reflected in a car window as he left Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.
Alberto Pezzali/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Alberto Pezzali/AP
London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

item.description:

First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
November 5, 202610:00 AM ET
Jennifer Ludden
A "for sale" sign is posted in front of a home on July 09, 2026 in Los Angeles, Calif. A new report finds generational wealth is helping a record share of first-time homebuyers pay with all cash.
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.
"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.
First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.

item.title: Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise -- especially girls
item.description:
Global Health
Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise — especially girls
November 5, 20267:24 AM ET
By
Jonathan Lambert
These soccer-loving Somali students are doing what health specialists want all teens to do daily — getting in some "moderate-to-vigorous" exercise.
Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images
The World Health Organization recommends adolescents spend at least one hour a day exercising enough to basically break a sweat — a brisk walk or a more intense pick-up soccer game. Lot's of research suggests this level of activity is crucial for supporting growing bodies and minds.
But new global data suggests only a small minority of kids and teens get that much. In fact, one in four report not hitting 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise any day of the week, according to a new study in The Lancet Global Health. Girls, as well as adolescents from middle- and lower-income countries reported even lower levels of exercise.

This could be a make-or-break week for President Trump's triumphal arch.
For months, the Trump administration has barreled toward his dream of building a 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C.: rubber-stamping and side-stepping various federal reviews, cutting out Congress and announcing imminent construction despite a lack of final approval and an ongoing legal battle.
In May, the entirely Trump-appointed Commission for Fine Arts approved the arch's design — still incomplete at the time. In September, a federal council packed with Trump allies abruptly terminated a historic preservation review that participants had already criticized as rushed.

item.title: As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards
item.description:
Economy
As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards
November 5, 20265:00 AM ET
By
Joe Hernandez
People study in the Rose Main Reading Room of the New York Public Library in midtown Manhattan on July 06, 2021.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Izzy Rivera reads at least one book every week, but buying them new isn't in her budget. As she saves up for law school, some expenses don't make the cut.
"Say I'm buying a few a month," she said, "it just isn't realistic."
That's why Rivera has recently been leaning more on local libraries near her home in Topeka, Kan., checking out both physical books and digital copies on the Libby app. (Some of her recent reads: Sour Cherry by Natalia Theodoridou, Spoilt Creatures by Amy Twigg and Plastic Inc. by Beth Gardiner.) Rivera also went to her library's used book sale last month, where she picked up 15 books for about $20.
The library's money-saving potential doesn't end there for her. Rivera also watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, reads the New York Times at no cost and often passes the time at a local branch.

A customer replaces the nozzle on a gasoline pump after making a purchase at Fuel City filling station Friday, April 17, 2026, in Dallas.
Tony Gutierrez/AP

Tony Gutierrez/AP
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help
Democrats are now poised to take control of Congress by wide margins — and a critical driver of their success has been voter fury about how the war in Iran has driven up the cost of fuel.
Before the war, about one fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. As the war throttled that waterway, the price of oil rose: A barrel of Brent crude cost about $70 in late February, spent months hovering around the $110 mark, and is now close to $95.
That's driven up the price of everything that's refined from crude. A gallon of gas costs $4.12 on average — about $1 higher than a year ago. The price of diesel hit a record high in September at $6.52, and while it's fallen a bit since then, a gallon remains about $2.50 higher than this time last year, according to AAA.
